_about: The salvation hub (plan 7.6f, second round). The words are the card's own: the Hebrew root ישׁע (the verb יָשַׁע 'save, deliver, give victory'; its nouns יְשׁוּעָה, יֵשַׁע, תְּשׁוּעָה, מוֹשָׁעוֹת) and the Greek σῴζω, σωτηρία, σωτήρ and σωτήριος, which the Greek Old Testament uses for the Hebrew. The frames carry the agent of only about a tenth of the Hebrew verb verses and no record at all of the participle ('Savior'), so the verb rows are made by hand where the text names who saves (the divine persons by hand), and by the verse's own words (in_verse) for the contested points. The contested points -- whether salvation can be lost, election and choice, faith and works, baptism, who is saved -- are set side by side, the text on each side, each with a note that the page takes no side. Built by tools/concepts/hub_build.py into out/concept-hubs/salvation.json.

titles.noun: What the text says of salvation

_words_why: The card's five (יָשַׁע, σῴζω, יְשׁוּעָה, σωτηρία, יֵשַׁע) and four more of the same family: תְּשׁוּעָה (the card listed it under 'other words', but it is the same root ישׁע and the Greek Old Testament renders it σωτηρία; Ps 40:10 and 51:14 stand beside the righteousness hub's 'Righteousness and salvation'), מוֹשָׁעוֹת (Ps 68:20, one verse), σωτήρ 'Savior' (24 verses) and σωτήριος 'saving' (5: Luke 2:30, 3:6, Acts 28:28, Eph 6:17, Titus 2:11). The Hebrew and the Greek are not said to be one word: every verse names the word it stands on. The Hebrew participle the Berean prints 'Savior' (Isa 43:11, Hos 13:4) is the verb יָשַׁע and is in the verb form, by hand, because the frames carry no record of it.
_sense_why: Measured on MACULA's gloss in each verse. Dropped as another sense: יָשַׁע at 1 Sam 25:26, 25:31, 25:33 ('avenging yourself') and Josh 22:22 ('spare'); everything else is the sense. 'help', 'victory' and 'preserve' stay for יָשַׁע because they are the same verb: the cry 'Help, my lord the king!' (2 Kgs 6:26), 'the LORD made David victorious' (2 Sam 8:6). σῴζω is 'healed' or 'made well' in 16 verses and stays, set in its own row, since it is the same Greek word the English prints two ways. One of the 77 verses of יְשׁוּעָה and one of the 45 of σωτηρία fall out as another sense.

others._why: Different words the English also renders save, deliver or rescue, named apart with their verses and never handed over as the same (as love names φιλέω). נָצַל 'rescue' is the Old Testament's other common word; ῥύομαι 'deliver' is the Greek one. Excluded: παραδίδωμι, נָתַן, ἔκδοτος, ἀναδίδωμι, שְׁלֵם, מָגַן -- the English 'deliver' there is 'hand over' ('delivered up', 'delivered into your hand'), not rescue.
others.title: Other words translated “save”, “deliver”, “rescue”

h5337.note: נָצַל means rescue, snatch away: a different word from יָשַׁע. The Berean prints “rescue” and “deliver” for it, and “save” in a few verses (Prov 14:25, “A truthful witness saves lives”). The page does not make the two words one.

g4506.note: ῥύομαι means rescue, draw out of danger: a different word from σῴζω. The Berean prints “deliver” and “rescue” (“deliver us from the evil one”, Matt 6:13; “rescued us from the dominion of darkness”, Col 1:13), and “the Deliverer” at Rom 11:26. The page does not make the two words one.

_review: Not yet reviewed. Written against the brief for the second round of hubs (2026-10-25): the contested points -- whether salvation can be lost ('Said as done' beside 'Said as still to come'), election and choice ('Who is saved', in the Bible's order), faith and works ('Saved, and faith', 'Saved, and works', 'Saved, and grace' as rule rows, one verse in every row it fits), baptism ('Saved, and baptism'), who is saved -- are rows of the text's own words with a note that the page takes no side; the divine persons are by hand (the LORD, Jesus, 'the Lord / Him' apart). 33 rows (21 verb, 12 noun): over the brief's 15-25, because the Hebrew verb and the Greek verb, the noun and the participle, are each a different record and the frames could not carry them; rows that could join if the owner wants fewer are named in the worker's report.

rows.label: The LORD saves his people and gives them victory
rows.note: Exod 14:30: “That day the LORD saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians”. The song that follows says “He has become my salvation” (Exod 15:2, in “Images of salvation”). Ps 106:8-10 says “He saved them”, “He rebuked the Red Sea” and “He saved them from the hand that hated them”.
rows._why: by hand (divine persons by hand): each verse names the LORD, God or 'your God', or is His own 'I will save'. The frames carry the agent for only 12 of the 100-odd Hebrew verses of this kind, so a rule row would have shown twelve. Ps 20:6 'saves His anointed' is here: the one saved is the king. Verses with no agent in the verse (Jer 23:6, 30:7, 33:16, 'Judah will be saved') are not: they stand in 'Said as still to come'. Hab 3:13 is a noun and is in 'Victory'. Zech 9:9 (the King 'righteous and victorious') is left under 'Every other use': whom it means is a reading the page does not make.

rows.label: The LORD saves the afflicted, the needy, the upright, those who take refuge in Him: “He saved me”
rows._why: by hand: each verse names the LORD or God, or addresses Him ('You save an afflicted people', Ps 18:27; 'You who save by Your right hand', Ps 17:7). Ps 7:10 and 17:7 are the Hebrew participle ('who saves'), which the frames do not carry. Ps 72:4 and 72:13 ('may he save the children of the needy') are the king's, and are under 'A person saves'.

rows.label: Asked of God: “Save me”, “Save us”, “Help, O LORD”
rows.note: In John 12:27 the request is weighed and set aside (“No, it is for this purpose that I have come to this hour”); Heb 5:7 says of Jesus that He offered prayers “to the One who could save Him from death”. “Lord, save me” (Matt 14:30) is in the row for “the Lord”.
rows._why: by hand: a command, a 'may You' or a 'we will cry out' made of the LORD or God: Ps 3:7 'Save me, O my God', Ps 118:25 'O LORD, save us'. Ps 12:1 'Help, O LORD' is the same verb. Ps 119:117 'Uphold me, and I will be saved' is the plea and its purpose. 1 Sam 7:8 is the people asking Samuel to keep asking. Hab 1:2 ('You do not save?') is a complaint, not a request, and is in 'Not saved'.

rows.label: “Savior”: “there is no Savior but Me”
rows.note: The Hebrew is the participle of the same verb as the rows above (“the one who saves”); the Berean prints “Savior”. The New Testament’s noun σωτήρ is a different word and is in the noun form.
rows._why: by hand: the frames carry no record of a participle, so none of these ten was in any row. Each names the LORD or God (Isa 63:8 'So He became their Savior' follows 'He said, They are surely My people'). Isa 62:11 ('your Savior comes') is the noun יֵשַׁע and is in the noun form.

rows.label: Jesus, the Son, Christ saves
rows.note: Where the verse says “I” or “Me” (John 5:34, 10:9, 12:47) it is Jesus speaking. Where it says “Him” or “no other name”, it is shown with the verse before, which names him: Acts 4:11–12, Rom 5:8–9, Heb 7:24–25; Rom 5:10 names “His Son”. “Lord, save us!” (Matt 8:25) and “Lord, save me!” (Matt 14:30) are cried to Jesus in the boat and on the water, shown with the verse before. Jude 5 reads “after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe”. In Jude 5 the Greek word on this page is κύριος, “Lord”; the Berean prints “Jesus”, and manuscripts differ.
rows._why: by hand (divine persons by hand): each verse names Jesus, Christ, the Son or the Son of Man, or is Jesus' own 'I' ('I have come ... to save the world', John 12:47). Acts 15:11 and 16:31 name 'the Lord Jesus'. Jude 5 is here because the Berean names Jesus; it is also a hard verse and stays. Rom 10:9 names Jesus but not as the one who saves; it is under 'Saved, and faith'.

rows.label: Saved by “the Lord”, “the One who is able”
rows.note: The text says “the Lord” and “the One who is able”; readers take these of the Father or of Christ (Acts 2:21 and Rom 10:13 quote “everyone who calls on the name of the LORD”, and Rom 10:9 says “Jesus is Lord”), and the page does not choose.
rows._why: Where the verse says only a title or a description, and neither it nor the verse before names whom, it is left unattributed. Jas 4:12 says 'the One who is able to save and destroy'. Doug, 2026-10-25: 'if the pronoun is resolved in the clause it should be treated as resolved'; so Acts 4:12 (4:11 'This Jesus'), Rom 5:9-10 (5:8 'Christ'; 5:10 'His Son') and Heb 7:25 (7:24 'Jesus') went to 'Jesus, the Son, Christ saves', each with the verse that names him. Matt 8:25 and 14:30 ('Lord, save us!', 'Lord, save me!') went to the Jesus row too. Doug, 2026-10-25: 'the statements were clearly directed at Jesus based on the prior sentences -- this a reasonable reading that is hard to say is controversial unless the original language is far different than the Berean'. It is not: 14:29 names Ἰησοῦν; in 8:24 the Greek has αὐτός ('He Himself') where the Berean prints 'Jesus', its referent named at 8:22, and 8:25 says they woke αὐτόν. Acts 2:21 and Rom 10:13 (quoting Joel's 'the name of the LORD') stay here: a text applied, not a pronoun resolved.

rows.label: A person saves, is asked to, or will not: a deliverer raised up, a king, a rescuer, a believer
rows._why: by hand: the verses where a person is the one who saves or is asked to. The Old Testament judges and kings are 'raised up' by the LORD (Judg 2:16, 3:9, 3:15, 2 Kgs 13:5) and the verse says so; the New Testament believers save others (1 Cor 9:22, 1 Tim 4:16, Jas 5:20, Jude 23). Judg 12:2-3, 2 Sam 10:19 and 1 Chr 19:19 are the refusals to help, and are in because the verb is there. 1 Cor 5:5 ('his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord') is not: who saves is not the person.

rows.label: Not saved: “no one to save”, “I will no longer save you”, “You do not save?”; and what cannot save: sword, horse, king, idol
rows.note: Some of these are the LORD's own words (Judg 10:13), some a complaint put to Him (Hab 1:2; Jer 14:9), the rest say that a king, a bow, a sword, an idol or a nation cannot save. Hos 1:7 and 1 Sam 17:47 (“not by sword or spear that the LORD saves”) are also in the LORD's row. The nouns (“so far from saving me”, “the help of man is worthless”) are in the noun form's “No salvation”.
rows._why: by hand: hard verses stay. Job 40:14 is the LORD's challenge ('your own right hand can save you'). Jer 8:20 is 'we have not been saved'. It was two rows (idols and kings; the LORD not saving) and is one: both say salvation is absent. The nouns (Ps 3:2, 22:1, 33:17, 60:11, 108:12, 119:155, 146:3, Isa 26:18, 59:11) were here and are moved to the noun form, so no verse stands in the verb form's row and the noun form's 'Every other use' at once.

rows.label: “He saved others; He cannot save Himself”: said to Jesus on the cross
rows.note: The words of the passers-by, the chief priests and scribes, the soldiers and one of the criminals, as the Gospels give them.
rows._why: by hand: a hard verse and a plain one. They say 'save' and the page says no more.

rows.label: Saved from uncleanness, sins, death, wrath; a life, a soul
rows._why: by hand: what the verse says the saving is from: 'from all your uncleanness' (Ezek 36:29), 'from all their apostasies' (Ezek 37:23), 'from their sins' (Matt 1:21), 'from wrath' (Rom 5:9), 'from death' (Heb 5:7; Jas 5:20), 'from this corrupt generation' (Acts 2:40); and the object of the verb that is the life or the soul (ψυχή, נֶפֶשׁ: Matt 16:25, Mark 3:4, Jas 1:21, Ps 72:13, Ps 109:31). Ps 68:20 is the noun ('our rescuer from death'). What the Hebrew saves from most often, the enemy, is the whole of 'The LORD saves his people and gives them victory'. Review 2026-10-25: this row and the former 'Save a life, a soul' were merged (both halves of the panel asked; Jas 5:20 stood in both). The Hebrew verses lead (panel b); the four examples are chosen so the label's items show (uncleanness, Ezek 36:29; soul and death, Jas 5:20; wrath, Rom 5:9; a life, Matt 16:25); 'this corrupt generation' (Acts 2:40) is in the row and no longer quoted in the label, since it is not among the four examples. The Greek is one word for life and soul: the Berean prints 'life' in Matt 16:25 and 'souls' in Jas 1:21. Luke 17:33 is περιποιέω, a different word, and is under the other words. Acts 27:20 and 27:31 (the ship) stay under 'Every other use': neither verse names a life or a soul.

rows.label: Where the Berean says “healed”, “made well”, “restore”: the same Greek word
rows.note: The Greek verb is σῴζω, the same as “saved” in the other rows; the Berean prints “healed”, “made well”, “get better”, “restore”. The page does not say which is meant where the English chose. Jesus’ “your faith has healed you” or “made you well” (Matt 9:22; Mark 5:34, 10:52; Luke 8:48, 17:19, 18:42) is here; Luke 7:50 and Luke 17:19 have the same Greek words (“your faith has ... you”), and the Berean prints “saved” in Luke 7:50 (in “Saved, and faith”) and “made well” in Luke 17:19.
rows._why: rule 6: one Greek word, two English renderings (as in the faith hub's 'saved or made well'). 16 verses where MACULA's gloss is 'healed', 'cured', 'made well'. They are kept out of 'Saved, and faith' by not_verses: that row's label says 'saved' and the Berean's English in them does not (found in the 16-verse check, Jas 5:15 'will restore the one who is sick'); here they carry 'faith' in the words shown.

rows.label: Saved, and faith, believing, trust, refuge

not_verses.Matt.27.42: the faith word is the mockers' 'we will believe in Him'; it is in the cross row (panel a, 2026-10-25)
not_verses.Matt.9.22: the Berean prints 'healed': it is in the healed row

not_verses.Luke.8.50: the Berean prints 'healed': it is in the healed row

not_verses.Luke.18.42: the Berean prints 'healed': it is in the healed row

rows.note: Set side by side with the rows on works, on grace and on baptism, as the text has them: a verse that names more than one stands in each. Where Christian traditions part on how faith, works and grace stand to being saved, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Saved, and works, deeds

not_verses.2Tim.4.18: ἔργον is 'every evil action' the Lord rescues him from, not works of the saved
not_verses.Hos.14.3: מַעֲשֶׂה here is 'the work of our own hands', the idols the people give up, not works of the saved

rows.note: Few verses with a word for “saved” also name works. Verses on works and being justified that have no such word are not shown here: Jas 2:24 (“a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone”), Rom 3:28 (“a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law”) and Gal 2:16. Eph 2:8, in the row above, is followed by “not by works, so that no one can boast” (2:9) and “created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (2:10); neither contains a word for “saved”, so they are named here and not shown. In 1 Cor 3:15 the Greek says “if anyone’s work is burned up”, and the Berean prints “If it is burned up”. Where Christian traditions part on how works stand to being saved, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Saved, and grace, mercy, compassion, loving devotion
Saved, and baptism
rows.note: Mark 16:16 stands in the longer ending (16:9-20) that the earliest manuscripts lack. A verse stands here only where being saved and baptism are in the same verse; verses side by side in the text (Acts 2:38-41; Acts 16:30-33) are not joined, and Titus 3:5 speaks of “the washing of new birth”, which readers take differently. Where Christian traditions part on what baptism has to do with being saved, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Said as done, or going on: “you have been saved”, “He saved us”, “those who are being saved”
rows.note: Set beside the next row as the text has them. How many verses stand in this row and the next follows which verses carry these verb forms, not the weight of either side. Rom 8:24 reads “For in this hope we were saved”; the verses of waiting for salvation (Gen 49:18; Lam 3:26) are in the noun form’s “Salvation: rejoicing, singing, waiting, longing, asking for it”. Where Christian traditions part on whether a person who has been saved can fall away, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Said as still to come, or to the end: “will be saved”, “if you hold firmly”, “to the end”
rows.note: Set beside the row above. How many verses stand in this row and the one above follows which verses carry these verb forms, not the weight of either side. Jer 23:6 and 33:16 (“Judah will be saved”) and Jer 30:7 (“Jacob’s distress, but he will be saved out of it”) are promises to Judah, Israel and Jacob; they stand here for the form of the verb and are not part of the question of falling away. Verses that speak of keeping or of falling away without a word for “saved” are not in this hub: “they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand” (John 10:28), “and then have fallen away” (Heb 6:6). Where Christian traditions part on whether a person who has been saved can fall away, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Asked, and what is said in reply: “Who then can be saved?”, “What must I do to be saved?”, “Turn to Me and be saved”, “Believe”
rows.note: The questions, then what the text says to do. Acts 15:1 is what some men from Judea were teaching (“Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved”), and Acts 15:11 (“through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved”) answers it. Jesus' answer to “Who then can be saved?” is in the next verse (Matt 19:26, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible”), which has no word for “saved”. Where Christian traditions part on faith, works, repentance and baptism, the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand, all in the one row so the questions and the answers are read together; the rows on faith, works and grace above are the rule rows (the verse's own words), this is the text asking and answering. Review 2026-10-25: 'Unless you are circumcised' is out of the label (both halves of the panel; none of the four examples showed it) and Acts 15:1 was held between the halves (b: keep it in the row; a: the note only). Doug, 2026-10-25, on the rulings sheet: 'as recommended' -- out of the row, quoted whole in the note beside its reply, Acts 15:11, so it is never read alone as one more thing to do. Prov 20:22 (waiting), Luke 8:12 (the devil taking the word) and 2 Thess 2:10 (refusing the love of the truth) are neither a question nor a reply and are out of this row; Prov 20:22 stays in 'The LORD saves the afflicted', Luke 8:12 is in 'Saved, and faith', 2 Thess 2:10 is under 'Every other use'. Mark 16:16 is marked once, in 'Saved, and baptism'. Acts 27:31 ('Unless these men remain with the ship, you cannot be saved') is a shipwreck and is not here.

rows.label: Who is saved, in the Bible's order: “all the ends of the earth” (Isa 45:22), “the elect” (Matt 24:22), “a few” (Luke 13:23), “the world” (John 3:17), “the remnant” (Rom 9:27), “all Israel” (Rom 11:26), “God chose you” (2 Thess 2:13), “everyone” (1 Tim 2:4)
rows.note: One list, in the Bible's order, and no reading first. “Chosen” (Mark 13:20; 2 Thess 2:13; 2 Tim 2:10) and “appointed” (1 Thess 5:9) stand beside “everyone” (1 Tim 2:4; Titus 2:11) and “the world” (John 3:17). Rom 9:27 and Rom 11:26 are Paul’s two statements about Israel, one verse each. Where Christian traditions part on election, free choice and who is saved, the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand. Was two rows ('Few, a remnant, the chosen' and 'Everyone, all, the world'); joined to stay near the row count, with the order the Bible's own so neither reading leads. Luke 3:6 and Titus 2:11 are the nouns, 2 Thess 2:13, 2 Tim 2:10 and 1 Thess 5:9 likewise.

rows.label: Every other use

not_verses.Acts.15.1: what some men from Judea were teaching; quoted whole in the note of 'Asked, and what is said in reply' beside its answer, Acts 15:11, so it is never read alone (Doug, 2026-10-25, rulings sheet item 1)

rows.note: Acts 27:20 and 27:31 are the ship in the storm (“we abandoned all hope of being saved”; “you cannot be saved”); 1 Sam 4:3 is the ark of the covenant (“so that it may go with us to save us”); 2 Thess 2:10 is “the love of the truth that would have saved them”. In Zech 9:9 the King comes “righteous and victorious”; whom the verse means the page does not say.

rows.label: God and salvation: “the salvation of the LORD”, “the God of my salvation”, “belongs to the LORD”, “God our Savior”
rows._why: 1 Tim 4:10 ('the living God, who is the Savior of everyone') names God in the verse and was left under 'Every other use' by the rule's distance; added by hand (rulings sheet, 2026-10-25, item 3). The by-hand row 'Salvation is the LORD's' (17 verses) is folded in through 'add' (Doug, 2026-10-25, rulings sheet: as recommended; Ps 3:8 'Salvation belongs to the LORD' and Rev 7:10 'Salvation to our God' say what 'the salvation of the LORD' says); Rev 7:10 is shown once. 2 Pet 1:1 is added by hand because the rule that placed Titus 2:13 here stops one word short of it (same ruling, the 'God and Savior' note).
rows.note: The text's own phrases, kept as written. Rev 7:10 reads “Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” Titus 2:13 (“our great God and Savior Jesus Christ”) and 2 Pet 1:1 (“our God and Savior Jesus Christ”) stand in both this row and “Jesus called Savior; salvation in Christ” because the phrase “God and Savior” is read of one person or of two; the page does not choose. In Titus the title Savior is given to God (1:3) and to Christ Jesus (1:4).

rows.label: Images of salvation: “my strength and my song”, “my light and my salvation”, “my rock”, “my shield”, “the horn of my salvation”
rows.note: “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation” is said in Exod 15:2 and again in Ps 118:14; Isa 12:2 has it as “the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and He also has become my salvation”. The row also holds the storehouse, the helmet, the garments, the cup, the walls and the wells of salvation.
rows._why: Review 2026-10-25: the label named thirteen things and the four examples showed four (panel a: cut the label to what is shown, or give each an example; panel b: relabel and put Exod 15:2 and Isa 12:2 first so the echo shows). Done: the label is the images the four examples show, Exod 15:2 and Isa 12:2 lead, and the note names the rest of what the row holds; the helmet keeps its own door. By hand, the text's own pairs: 'my light and my salvation', 'the Rock of my salvation', 'horn of my salvation', 'shield of salvation', 'helmet of salvation', 'garments of salvation', 'cup of salvation', 'springs of salvation', 'chariots of salvation'. It was a rule row on rock, light and strength and a pick row of the helmet; the rule took Isa 49:6 ('a light for the nations') and 2 Chr 6:41 ('the ark of Your might') and they are joined here so only what the verse says is in. Isa 60:18 ('you will name your walls Salvation') is a name.

rows.label: Proclaimed, revealed, sent to the nations; near and coming: “the day of salvation”
rows._why: by hand: 'proclaim His salvation day after day', 'the message of salvation', 'the gospel of your salvation', 'all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God', 'salvation has come to the Gentiles', 'My salvation is coming soon', 'the salvation that is ready to be revealed'. Was three rows (proclaimed, the nations, near and coming) and is one, to stay near the row count.

rows.label: Salvation, and works, obedience, repentance, the commandments: worked out, inherited, obtained, neglected
rows.note: Set beside the next row's faith, as the text has them: Phil 2:12 says “work out your salvation with fear and trembling”; Heb 5:9 “the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him”; 2 Cor 7:10 “repentance that leads to salvation”; Heb 2:3 “how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?”. Where Christian traditions part on how works stand to being saved, the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the verses where the human side is in the verse with the noun: doing (Isa 56:1, Phil 2:12), obeying (Heb 5:9), repenting (Acts 5:31, 2 Cor 7:10), carrying out the commandments (Ps 119:166), inheriting, obtaining, growing in, neglecting. The rule row on ἔργον, ὑπακούω and μετάνοια found four verses; the Hebrew and the 'inherit' verses were missing.

rows.label: Salvation, and faith, believing, trust, refuge

not_verses.Titus.1.3: πιστεύω here is 'entrusted' (the proclamation entrusted to me), not believe
not_verses.Titus.2.10: πίστις here is 'good faith', the slaves' fidelity, not faith in God
not_verses.Ps.146.3: 'Put not your trust in princes ... who cannot save': trust and saving are named but the verse says not to trust; it is in 'Not saved'

rows.note: Set side by side with the previous row, as the text has them. Where Christian traditions part on how faith and works stand to being saved, the page takes no side.

rows.label: Salvation and righteousness
rows.note: Rom 1:16, in “Salvation, and faith”, is followed by Rom 1:17: “the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish”. Rom 1:17 has no word for salvation, so it is named here and not shown.

rows.label: Salvation: rejoicing, singing, waiting, longing, asking for it
rows._why: by hand: 'rejoice in Your salvation', 'I await Your salvation', 'wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD', 'My soul faints for Your salvation', 'I long for Your salvation', 'grant us Your salvation', 'my heart's desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is for their salvation' (Rom 10:1). A rule on the Hebrew words for joy and hope found 21 of these; the others use words the rule did not list (שָׂשׂוֹן in Ps 51:12, שִׂבֵּר in Ps 119:166, יָחַל in Lam 3:26).

rows.label: Victory and deliverance from enemies: “a great victory”, “a great deliverance”
rows._why: by hand: the nouns for victory, the Hebrew תְּשׁוּעָה and יְשׁוּעָה as the Berean prints them 'victory', 'victories', 'deliverance'. Prov 11:14 ('with many counselors comes deliverance') is not about enemies and stays under 'Every other use'. Acts 7:25 is God using Moses 'to deliver them' from Egypt.

rows.label: No salvation: “God will not deliver him”, “so far from saving me”, “salvation is far”, “the help of man is worthless”
rows.note: Ps 22:1 begins “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”; the Gospels give those words as Jesus’ cry (Matt 27:46; Mark 15:34). The page draws nothing further.
rows._why: by hand: the nouns of the verb form's 'Not saved'. Hard verses stay: Ps 3:2 is what others say of the psalmist; Ps 22:1 a cry to God; Ps 33:17 ('A horse is a vain hope for salvation') and 146:3 (princes 'who cannot save'); Isa 26:18 ('We have given no salvation to the earth').

rows.label: Jesus called Savior; salvation in Christ
rows.note: Acts 4:12 (“Salvation exists in no one else”) follows “This Jesus is ‘the stone you builders rejected’” (4:11), and Acts 5:31 (“God exalted Him … as Prince and Savior”) follows “The God of our fathers raised up Jesus” (5:30); each is shown with the verse that names him. Titus 2:13 (“our great God and Savior Jesus Christ”) and 2 Pet 1:1 (“our God and Savior Jesus Christ”) stand in both this row and “God and salvation” because the phrase “God and Savior” is read of one person or of two; the page does not choose. In Titus the title Savior is given to God (1:3) and to Christ Jesus (1:4).
rows._why: by hand (divine persons by hand): each verse names Jesus, Christ or the Son as Savior or as the one in whom salvation is, or says 'Him' where the verse before names him. Doug, 2026-10-25 (rulings sheet, items 2 and 3): 'if the pronoun is resolved in the clause it should be treated as resolved -- general rule revision -- list both verses together if needed'; 'Acts 4:11 sets clear context -- it is clearly a Jesus reference'. So Acts 4:12 and 5:31 are here, each with the verse that names him (4:11, 5:30); 5:31 also stays under 'works, repentance', for the repentance it names. Titus 2:13 and 2 Pet 1:1 read 'our great God and Savior Jesus Christ'. 2 Pet 3:2 ('our Lord and Savior') names no one in the verse or the one before it, and stays under 'Every other use'.
